Both my roommates are saying I’m being an asshole and that it’s the least I can do because I have the best room in the house because it’s the most separate. Scenario:
AITA for playing music in the middle of the day when my roommate has a weird sleep schedule? | So I live in a 3 bedroom duplex with 2 other girls. The duplex is laid out with two bedrooms up stairs with a bathroom in the middle. Downstairs is the living room, kitchen, dining room and roomates room and her own bathroom. When we picked rooms I picked first because I moved in first and then my roommate upstairs picked and then the girl downstairs. She wasn’t too happy with her room because it was the smallest and the location but settled because she had her own bathroom. So the roommate downstairs has a very weird schedule. Sometimes she works nights and sometimes mornings. Sometimes she has 5 hour days and other days she can work 13. So obviously with the constant changing work schedule her sleeping schedule has became very weird and erratic and we never know when she’s asleep now. So since I can never guess when she’s asleep I often so downstairs in the kitchen and make food and play music on my speaker while I meal prep. It’s apart of my routine through out the day that i really enjoy since I don’t work till 2pm. But yesterday my roommate downstairs texted our group chat and asked us to please stop playing music in the kitchen at any time of the day. She said it wakes her up almost every time and when she is a wake it’s just very disruptive. My other roommate said sure but I said that’s not really fair because she often plays music too in the kitchen. She told me it wasn’t really fair that she had the shittiest room in the house and that if I wanted to switch with her so she wouldn’t have to be woken up by it that would be fine. Of course I said no and said I was going to keep playing music because it’s noon usually when I do it and it’s ridiculous I have to step around her schedule. Both my roommates are saying I’m being an asshole and that it’s the least I can do because I have the best room in the house because it’s the most separate. I honestly think they are being assholes because why should I have to be so quiet I’m the middle of the day!?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: This is a **0** (not AITA) scenario—but with some nuance. Here’s why: ### **The Core Issue: Fairness vs. Personal Habits** 1. **Your Routine is Valid (But Not Absolute)** - Playing music while meal prepping is a reasonable way to enjoy your time, especially if you work later in the day. However, **your routine doesn’t override your roommate’s need for rest**, even if her schedule is unpredictable. - The fact that *she* also plays music in the kitchen doesn’t negate the fact that *her* music disrupts *your* sleep (if that were the case). Consistency matters—if she’s okay with her noise levels, she shouldn’t expect you to be. 2. **The Room Situation is Relevant (But Not a Get-Out-of-Jail-Free Card)** - Your roommate’s complaint about the room layout is **valid**—she got the smallest, least ideal space, and now she’s dealing with noise disruption. That’s a legitimate frustration. - However, **your room’s "separation" doesn’t mean you’re exempt from basic courtesy**. If the duplex layout means her room is closer to the kitchen (where noise travels), that’s a shared responsibility to manage. 3. **The "Middle of the Day" Argument is Weak** - You say it’s "ridiculous" to adjust for noon, but **noise tolerance varies**. Some people are light sleepers, some are deep sleepers, and some (like your roommate) have erratic schedules that make them more sensitive to disruptions. - If she’s asking for quiet *most* of the time (not just when she’s sleeping), that’s a reasonable request—not an unreasonable demand. 4. **The Offer to Switch Rooms is a Red Herring** - She suggested trading rooms as a solution, but **that’s not a fair ask**. You didn’t choose the layout, and switching wouldn’t fix the noise issue—it would just move the problem elsewhere. - If she’s unhappy with her room, the solution should be **shared** (e.g., negotiating with the landlord, adjusting the lease, or finding a compromise in noise levels). ### **Why You’re Being Perceived as the "Asshole"** - **You dismissed her feelings** ("it’s ridiculous I have to step around her schedule") without considering that her schedule is *exactly* why she needs quiet. - **You didn’t offer a compromise**—even a small one (e.g., lowering volume, playing music only when she’s awake, or using headphones). - **You framed it as an unfair burden** ("I have the best room") without acknowledging that *she* also has a valid complaint about her living situation. ### **How to Fix This (Without Being a Doormat)** 1. **Acknowledge the Problem** - *"I hear you—her schedule is unpredictable, and I shouldn’t assume she’s awake just because it’s noon. I’ll try lowering the volume or playing music only when I know she’s up."* 2. **Find a Middle Ground** - Maybe you can **use headphones** when she’s likely sleeping (check her schedule if she shares it). - Or **set a rule** (e.g., "No loud music after 10 AM unless we know she’s awake"). 3. **Don’t Use the Room as an Excuse** - Your room being "better" doesn’t mean you get to ignore basic living standards. If she’s struggling, **you’re part of the solution**, not the problem. ### **Final Verdict: 0 (Not AITA, but You Could Do Better)** You’re not *wrong* for enjoying music, but **you’re not being considerate enough** of your roommate’s needs. A little flexibility goes a long way in shared living. Would you like help drafting a response to your roommates? Or tips on how to negotiate noise levels in a duplex?
